hints: Focus on the two separate halide tests here, the fumes with concentrated sulfuric acid and the colour plus ammonia solubility of the silver halide precipitate.
Steamy white fumes that give a white precipitate soluble in dilute ammonia point specifically to hydrogen chloride and silver chloride.
Now ask which starting solid could supply chloride ions and also dissolve easily in water to fit the first description.
walkthrough:
**Decode the fumes with concentrated sulfuric acid**

Think of this as the acid displacing a more volatile hydrogen halide from the solid. White steamy fumes mean hydrogen chloride, $HCl$, was formed.

$$\text{Cl}^- (s) + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(l) \rightarrow \text{HCl}(g) + \text{HSO}_4^-$$

**Decode the silver nitrate test**

The $HCl$ gas dissolves and gives $\text{Cl}^-$ ions, which form a white precipitate of silver chloride with silver nitrate.

$$\text{Ag}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgCl}(s) \text{ white precipitate}$$

**Use ammonia solubility to confirm the halide**

Remember the key distinction: $\text{AgCl}$ is white and dissolves in dilute $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{AgBr}$ is cream and needs concentrated $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{AgI}$ is yellow and insoluble. Soluble in dilute ammonia confirms chloride.

**Choose a soluble chloride solid for Q**

Q itself is described as white crystalline and dissolves easily in water. That fits a soluble Group 1 chloride like sodium chloride, $\text{NaCl}$, and rules out insoluble chlorides.

options.A: AgCl does contain chloride, but it is a white precipitate that is insoluble in water. It does not dissolve easily, so it cannot be Q.
options.B: NaBr is soluble and white, but bromide behaves differently. With concentrated sulfuric acid it gives steamy HBr fumes followed by brown bromine vapour, and with silver nitrate it gives a cream precipitate of AgBr which is insoluble in dilute ammonia.
options.C: NaCl fits all three clues. It is white and very soluble in water. With concentrated sulfuric acid it gives steamy white HCl fumes, which give white AgCl precipitate that dissolves in dilute ammonia to form [Ag(NH3)2]+.
options.D: PbBr2 is a bromide, not a chloride, so it would give a cream AgBr precipitate insoluble in dilute ammonia. It is also only sparingly soluble in cold water, not easily soluble, and lead bromide is usually cream rather than white.
